newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries a bit higher at midday, dollar cited.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries a bit higher at midday, dollar cited.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries were narrowly higher at midday on Monday, aided by some short-covering and a slight bounce of the dollar off its mid-morning lows, traders said.
"The fact that we bounced a little bit on the dollar helped out a lot," said Matthew Alexy, chief markets strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
Treasury prices opened mostly unchanged on Monday and dipped about 1/8 of a point on the 30-year bond before gradually erasing that loss and edging into the plus column.
In early afternoon dealings, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 3/32 to 93-23/32, yielding 7.14 percent.
Five-year notes were up 1/32 to 99-5/32, yielding 6.83 percent and 10-year notes were up 1/32 to 95-5/32, yielding 6.94 percent.

The only economic data the market got on Monday were stronger than forecast February and March new single-family home sales. Economists had told Reuters the data would show that new single-family home sales occurred at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 794,000 in March, down from a 811,000 rate in February.
Instead, sales occurred at an annualized rate of 813,000, the Commerce Department said, down 2.5 percent from February's upwardly revised 834,000 annualized rate.

Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi, said the market's ability to firm after the strong home sales figures showed there "might be an underlying bid to the market," though not a big one.
"The market is doing the right thing if you want to be long," he said. "It behaved well on what should have been bearish news."
Another positive sign for longs was the market's ability to draw support at 7.16 percent, the yield that the 30-year long bond rose to on April 4 after the March employment report, Rupkey said.
Still, analysts agreed that the market was bound to narrow ranges ahead of key economic data due this week.

"Right now everybody is totally focused on the next four days," said William Hornbarger, fixed-income strategist at A.G. Edwards & Sons. "You have important numbers every single morning. People are kind of holding onto their hats to see what comes next."

Participants fear that starting with Tuesday's release of the first-quarter Employment Cost Index (ECI), those data will emphasize a robust economy and push Federal Reserve policy makers toward boosting interest rates again at the May 20 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).

Economists polled by Reuters forecast a 0.9 percent rise in the first-quarter ECI. A 1.0-percent rise or more would hurt the market, traders said. But a rise of just 0.8 percent could spur a "relief" rally.
"If you get a softer number, certainly it will bring some short-covering into the market," said Hornbarger.
But Hornbarger said any rally on Tuesday would be "limited by the fact that more key numbers are coming."

Other key data set for release later this week include the first-quarter Gross Domestic Product (GDP), expected to be up 4.1 percent, the April National Association of Purchasing Management's (NAPM) index, and the government's payroll employment data for April.

Two-year notes were up 1/32 to 99-23/32, yielding 6.53 percent. Three-month bill rates were up four basis points to 5.20 percent. Six-month bill rates were up three basis pints to 5.43 percent. Year bill rates were down one basis point to 5.73 percent. (( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679 ))
